abstract: The benefits of incretin agonists, including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists, are largely attributed to glycemic control and weight loss, as these therapies enhance insulin secretion, suppress glucagon release and delay gastric emptying to produce satiety. Yet treatment is also associated with lower risk of cardiometabolic, renal and other chronic diseases. Whether these broader benefits depend on weight loss itself or reflect direct effects of treatment on physiology remains unclear, as does the basis of the marked variation in how patients respond. Resolving these questions has been difficult because weight loss and drug effects occur together, and because molecular studies of treated patients have been limited in scope. Here we profiled paired plasma samples collected before and after treatment from 165 individuals drawn from DynamiQ, a biorepository that links plasma samples to longitudinal clinical records, combining mass spectrometry-based proteomics, a targeted inflammation proteomics panel (NULISAseq) and non-targeted metabolomics to capture metabolic function, inflammation and markers of chronic disease. Treatment was associated with broad remodeling of the plasma proteome and metabolome, but the extent to which this remodeling depended on weight loss differed across the molecular layers. The metabolome carried a lipid signature that scaled with the weight lost, whereas proteomic and inflammation-panel changes largely did not depend on weight loss. Among these changes, treatment was associated with lower circulating mitochondrial oxidative proteins and cardiolipins, consistent with relief of lipid-driven metabolic stress, and with a shift of the inflammation panel toward a less inflamed state. A metabolic aging clock showed that age acceleration decreased by a mean of 2.96 years after treatment (95% confidence interval -4.95 to -0.98; P = 3.7 x 10-3), a change that did not depend on weight loss or on the interval between samples, with the largest reductions in participants starting from the highest age acceleration, most of whom had diabetes. Treatment-associated features overlapped with features associated with cardiometabolic, renal and hepatic disease. Before treatment, higher systemic inflammation, reflecting chronic tissue stress and repair, was associated with less subsequent weight loss. Together, these findings indicate that incretin agonist treatment is associated with lower markers of metabolic and inflammatory stress and with a younger metabolic age, changes that do not depend on weight loss, identify baseline inflammation as an axis of heterogeneity in treatment response, and suggest that biorepositories linking longitudinal multi-omic profiling to clinical records can relate drug pharmacodynamics to disease risk and to variation in patient response.
